## Ch9's exercise: Batch process

This script is just to cluster the epochs by conditions and save the dataset after renaming them. So not too hard to program.

```{MATLAB Ch9_batch, eval = F}
file_list = {
    'umeeg101', '.set';
    'umeeg103', '.set'};
conditions = {
    '201', '202', '203';
    'irrelevant', 'relevant', 'odd'};

% 额外练习1无非也就是嵌套循环，给来自每个被试的数据分epoch以后
% 修改文件头，然后改名存储
for i = 1:size(file_list, 1)

    % 加载文件
    % 但是注意一下，这一步即需要.set也需要.fdt文件
    EEG = pop_loadset('filename', ...
        [file_list{i, 1}, '_10_Pruned_with_ICA', file_list{i, 2}], ...
        'filepath', '.');

    for j = 1:size(conditions, 2)

        % 对每个文件进行condition条件的分类和数据提取
        cEEG = pop_selectevent( EEG, 'latency','-1<=1', ...
            'type', conditions{1, j}, ...
            'deleteevents', 'off', ...
            'deleteepochs', 'on', ...
            'invertepochs', 'off');

        % 提取出来以后修改文件头
        cEEG = pop_editset(cEEG, ...
            'setname', [file_list{i, 1} '_' conditions{1, j}], ...
            'subject', file_list{i, 1}, ...
            'condition', conditions{2, j});

        %保存文件
        pop_saveset(cEEG, [file_list{i, 1} '_' conditions{1, j} file_list{i, 2}]);
    end
end


%%
% 其实还有一个对另一个条件的个体历遍处理
% 就是先选出202 和 201的epochs
% 然后在进一步选择呈现的照片类型
% 然后在分relevant和irrelevant
% 最后editset修改相关信息，比如group参数标注照片类型，再保存数据
% 不过我懒，今天没有动力，效率也不高，直接进入下一章算了
% 唉算了还是搞了把就当练习控制语句了

file_list = {
    'umeeg103', '.set';
    'umeeg101', '.set'};
conditions = {
    '201', '202', '203';
    'irrelevant', 'relevant', 'odd'};
self = {'self', 'other'};

for i = 1:size(file_list, 1)

    % 加载数据
    EEG = pop_loadset('filename', ...
        [file_list{i, 1}, '_10_Pruned_with_ICA', file_list{i, 2}], ...
        'filepath', '.');

    % 先去除无关条件，就是动物的那个203
    EEG = pop_selectevent(EEG, 'latency','-1<=1', ...
        'type', {'201', '202'}, ...
        'deleteevents', 'off', ...
        'deleteepochs', 'on', ...
        'invertepochs', 'off');

    % 然后开始分类我他条件
    for j = 1:length(self)

        % 不同条件那肯定得进行不同的删选
        % 然后自我照片的marker是1
        if j == 1
            cEEG = pop_selectevent(EEG, 'latency','-200<=0', ...
                'type', {'1'}, ...
                'deleteevents', 'off', ...
                'deleteepochs', 'on', ...
                'invertepochs', 'off');
        else
            cEEG = pop_selectevent(EEG, 'latency','-200<=0', ...
                'type', {'1'}, ...
                'deleteevents', 'off', ...
                'deleteepochs', 'on', ...
                'invertepochs', 'on');
        end

        % 然后改一下文件头
        cEEG = pop_editset(cEEG, ...
            'group', self{j});

        % 然后进一步把相关不相关的条件给选出来
        % 然后这一步有个try catch语句可以留意一下
        % 这个语句就是加入报错就执行备用方案
        % 因为自我*相关的各个条件的trial不一定够，
        % 这一步分epoch可能就中间不知道哪里报错
        % 然后用try catch语句执行，报错返回一个信息然后执行下一个文件

        for k = 1:2
            % 因为只要分类201 202，所以这里就1:2


            try
                cEEG = pop_selectevent(cEEG, 'latency','-1<=1', ...
                    'type', conditions{1, k}, ...
                    'deleteevents', 'off', ...
                    'deleteepochs', 'on', ...
                    'invertepochs', 'off');

                % 修改文件头和保存文件
                ccEEG = pop_editset(cEEG, ...
                    'setname', [file_list{i, 1} '_' self{j} '_' conditions{1, k}], ...
                    'group', self{j}, ...
                    'condition', conditions{2, k});

                pop_saveset(ccEEG, ...
                    [file_list{i, 1} '_' self{j} '_' conditions{1, k} file_list{i, 2}]);

            catch ME
                % 然后是如果报错怎么办
                % 不耽误它跳过然后执行下一个loop
                disp (ME.message)
                disp ('Probably not enough rel_self epochs!');
                fprintf('Error processing file: %s, condition: %s\n', file_list{i, 1}, conditions{1, k});
                
            end
        end
    end
end
```

# Ch10 Average analysis

## Visualizing multi-subject data

Because there is a individual difference in event-related potential for the same task, we need to do a **<font color = 'red'>grand average</font>**, namely average across subjects, to make a scientific conclusion. Since we have averaged the potential across epochs, the current operation is called "grand average", meaning we are averaging the averaged individual ERP.

To do so, we rely on the `STUDY` structure of eeglab, which helps not only ERPs, but also time/frequency analysis. Besides, it provides way to conduct basic statistical analysis for one-way or two-way design.

### Create the study design in eeglab

In the last chapter we aggregated all conditions into one mixed dataset to create a controlled condition (regardless the conditions). For this chapter, we will use the **<font color = 'red'>minimal control condition</font>**, namely use a condition with minimal manipulation as a baseline. Specifically, it's loading all `*_irr.set` (but it's pity that I can't use the format of "*_irr.set" to search the file in Finder) first into the eeglab.

Then click `File > Create Study > Using all loaded dataset`. Then we can name the new study and check the condition & group label. Press "OK" if everything is done. The principle is make sure the name of condition and group is **consistent**, otherwise the eeglab would mistakenly recognize your experimental design. If we have written the information correctly by `pop_editset()` at the previous steps, all these will be filled automatically in current the dialogue.

![**Fig 10.1** Create a study](./note_image/Ch10_create_study.png)

<br>

One thing special then is that Spapé used a group of samples with different number of channels. Therefore we need to fix it up, interpolating the values of missing channels (e.g., there are 34 channels for `umeeg101` whereas 64 channels for `umeeg102`). Click `Study > Precompute channel measures`. In the pop-out dialogue, according to Spapé, leave the ICA-related item unchecked, and no necessity to specify the parameters here. Although **the function of precomputation is to calculate the values required by latter visualization, <font color = 'red'>in advance</font>**.

![**Fig 10. 2** Aligning the channel number by interpolation](./note_image/Ch10_interpolation.png)

<br>

### Looking at grand average ERPs

Click `Study > Plot channel measures` and choose the command on the left or the right panel (see figure 10.2.). However the outliers has a worse effect on the average potential as it's a series of average point that is correlated in time and space.

![**Fig 10.2** Aligning the channel number by interpolation](./note_image/Ch10_plot.png)

<br>

The correlation between channels interferes the independent assumption of statistics and amplifies the effect of outlier on the analysis (one channel contaminates the rest part of data from other electrodes). Moerover, bad data also pollutes the later timepoints, especially the low-pass filter of 80 Hz has been applied. 即离群值在时间和空间上的污染.

> Generally, EEG has greater power in lower (such as 2 - 10 Hz) frequency than higher frequency, so the its activities are quite similar within earlier period like 50 ms (1000 ms / 20 Hz).

The outlier is one with potential beyond more than $\pm$ 2 standard deviation from the average level. Once a true outlier is detected, we should go back to the previous steps to see if any problem could have been solved such as reject more artifacts.

Then use the skills from chapter 9 to identify the components by plot at the group level. For example, recognize the basic components like P1, N1, P2 and N2; and the components different between conditions. <font color = 'red'>But how to create topoplot matrix instead of a single plot at population level???</font>

## Time/frequency analysis

EEG is a sum (synchronization and de-synchronization) of oscillation at frequency bands. A new one synchronization or the stopping of the old synchronization (de-synchronization)? For instance, the event-related de-synchronization of $\alpha$ rhythm is a signal of being active.

```{MATLAB Ch10_EEG_music, eval = F}
% first load a epoched dataset
% I used umeeg101 for this
EEG = pop_loadset( ...
    'filename', 'umeeg101_10_Pruned_with_ICA.set', ...
    'filepath', '.');


% this command will play the sound composed by the channel 5 and 8, all
% timepoints of the first epoch
sound(EEG.data([5 18], :, 1));


% if we have loaded a study set, we can use the command below
sound(ALLEEG(1).data([5 18],:,1))
```

The idea is that, to find out the link between mind and brain, we can use the **<font color = 'red'>Fourier transformation</font>** onto the EEG data, so that decomposing the time series into a frequency spectrum, allowing us to see the contribution of each frequency band to the power. Pure Fourier transformation loses time information so it tells a little about event-related thing. However, by applying **<font color = 'red'>time/frequency analysis</font>**, we still keep the temporal precision when decomposing the EEG signal into spectral properties.

time field -> frequency field

**<font color = 'red'>Wavelet analysis (小波浪分析?)</font>** is a common way to achieve time/frequency analysis. This technique roughly uses a template/model of a wave, whose frequency is defined by its shape changing, to compare or match the potential wave of actual signal. The more it mated, the greater power is at a certain frequency. 这个玩意就是用一个波形模版，这个模板可以通过拉伸改变频率，去跟你原始信号进行比对。然后实际信号和不同频率的模板比对得越匹配，说明这个频率的功率越高。然后功率高低用颜色表示，纵轴表示频率，时间横轴得以被保留。

![**Fig 10.3** The principle of wavelet analysis](./note_image/Ch10_wavelet.png)

<br>

### Spetrum analysis

Click `Study > Precompute channel measures` and enable the option of `Power spectrum` in the pop-out dialogue. Press `Test` to see a pilot spectum plot for the first 20 trials of the first participant.

![**Fig 10.3** The principle of wavelet analysis](./note_image/Ch10_spectrum_precompute.png)

<br>

The point of pilot plot is to see whether the resolution of the picture fits the research question. Specifically, if we are interested in the neural activities around 6.5 to 7 Hz, data should be found within this frequency bands. And

- The lower limit of frequency = $\frac{1}{\text{time window of analysis (s)}}$
- The upper limit of frequency = $\frac{\text{sample rate}}{2}$

Then we want to see the spectrum plot for the whole study set. Click `Study > Plot channel measures`. We can set the certain range of frequency (e.g., 0 - 80 Hz) to plot by click the `Params` near `Plot spectra`. 

![**Fig 10.4** Spectrum plot for the whole study set](./note_image/Ch10_spectrum_plot.png)

<br>

The $\alpha$ rhythm is easy to see on the spectrum plot. Apart from that, the $\alpha$ can also be seen on the topoplot by clicking `Params` near the `Plot spectra`, set `Frequency` within 7 - 12 Hz, and select `Plot averaged topography over frequency range` (multiple channels need to be selected). We can see the increasing $\alpha$ power around parieto-occipital region, consistent with classical theory of $\alpha$ wave. The point is, it's always better to compare topoplot for **<font color = 'red'>multiple frequency under different conditions</font>** rather than simply "where is it". 频谱图最有意义的是条件差异 (**<font color = 'red'>condition contrast</font>**).

![**Fig 10.5** Topoplot for $\alpha$ power](./note_image/Ch10_topo_alpha.png)

<br>

### Time/frequency analysis

To conduct this analysis. Same as before, `Precompute` -> `Plot`. But we need to adjust parameters of `ERSPs` or `ITCs` for time/frequency analysis.

|indicator|what is reflected|meaning|symbol in the plot|
|---|---|---|---|
|`ERSPs`|power 功率|参与该频段的神经元数量是否增加|红=ERS，蓝=ERD|
|`ITCs`|phase-locking 相位同步|神经元是否在同一时间点对齐相位|黄/红=高同步|

- ERS = Event‑Related Synchronization
- ERD = Event‑Related Desynchronization

![**Fig 10.6** Pre-computation for wavelet analysis](./note_image/Ch10_wavelet_precom.png)

<br>

Given the core of wavelet analysis is actually match waveform with some kinds of template, one issue is that the lower frequency may has lower temporal resolution because the slow wavelet's long cycle exceeds the time window of analysis. One illustration is, if we employ a wavelet with 1 Hz (has its cycle of 333 ms) onto a epoch in which the stimulus onset is at 200 ms, the first wavelet is from -200 to 133 ms, across the onset time. This may be confusing for us to figure out whether that wavelet is resulted from the stimulus. However, too fast wavelet also gives arise of other issue: it may capture many random spike instead of interested oscillation.

So, how to choose a good enough wavelet to conduct our analysis? "It depends"... Spapé gave some principles: **pursue the optimal temporal resolution by testing out different number of cycles**. For example, use 1 cycle for lower frequency and increase the cycle for higher frequency. To do so, time to change the parameters into:

```{MATLAB Ch10_wavelet_precom, eval = F}
'cycles', [1 0.5], 'nfreqs', 50, 'maxfreq', 80, 'ntimesout', 50

% 'cycles', [1 0.5] 改变周期数，这里是个数组，低频周期从1开始，高频周期0.5结束
% 'nfreqs', 50 设定总共跑几个wavelets
% 'maxfreq', 80 设定wavelet的频率上限，这里80，和我们的感兴趣频段与低通滤波一致
% 'minfreq' 虽然这段代码没有，不过值得一说，eeglab默认最低频率是3 Hz
% 'ntimesout', 50 保留时间点的数量，原本不是1秒512个时间点吗，Spapé为了节省算力
```

### Comparing conditions in a one-way design

Now we need to create a study set containing both of `irr` and `rel` conditions. `Study > Plot channel measures` after pre-computation. Some parameters need to be set for making it easier to make comparison between plots under two conditions (see the figure 10.6).

![**Fig 10.6** Comparing the potential under conditions](./note_image/Ch10_conpare_condition_plot.png)

<br>

So far we have inspect the data always by visualization and naked eyes, but too much randomness in such analysis that is non-replicable. So we need to carry out the statistical things with carefulness in the next chapter. Spapé introduced some **<font color = 'red'>problematic statistics</font>** here. I think this "bad" stat may be a way to explore the data and hypothesis in the real-life practice, as He Zhenhong did so.

> "a solid effect in the main contrast doesn’t generally disappear – the way that vague, non-replicable effects do sometimes appear by applying questionable statistics"

Click `Study > Plot channel measures > STAT params`, and use `parametric statistics` with the threshold of `0.001`. Don't forget enable "plot first variable on the same panel". Then press the `Plot` button will return you the results.

![**Fig 10.6** This is bad statistical operation](./note_image/Ch10_bad_one_way.png)

This section is about conduct 2 $\times$ 2 design analysis. Remember in the end of the last chapter, we used batch script to separate epochs into 4 categories? That is. It's pity that eeglab isn't component to create a good plot for such design, Spapé thereby suggested use other software and would talk about it in the chapter 11.

![**Fig 10.7** 2 $\times$ 2 design with urgly plots](./note_image/Ch10_multi_factorial.png)

### Interpreting differences in the ERP

**<font color = 'red'>Region of interest (ROI)</font>**? Clusters? Going through the plot channel measures? Couldn't Spapé do this part step by step? Can't understand the aim and meaning of this part and what are the output used for? Of course I know is to test the hypothesis.

In this section, just for tutorial, Spapé went through a plenty of contrast plot and note the significant time range down, then summarize the clusters from electrodes of interest (ROI). It's similar with the skill to define the component in chapter 9. Once a cluster which is spatial and temporally continuous is defined, we can just pick up the most representative channel to analyze.

Spapé then introduce some mistakes in attributing the cause of difference.

#### Different baseline or ERPs

- 如果你在 ERP 的非常早期看到条件差异，那通常是 baseline 出问题

- 如果在 ERP 的非常晚期看到奇怪的bump，那通常是因为下一张刺激或黑屏本身引发了新的视觉 ERP

- 而在选择反应任务中，反应时差异会进一步污染 ERP。

- 最终结论：ERP 必须结合“物理上下文”（刺激序列、黑屏、反应时、任务结构）来解释，而不能只盯着成分本身。

This length of baseline affects the rest part of EEG signals, so the longer one has more reliability to some extent. However, the baseline itself is influenced by more factors than mere its length. For example, in current experiment of tutorial, a relevant stimulus can only following irrelevant stimulus; whereas an irrelevant stimulus following either relevant or irrelevant images. Give our epoch is from -200 to 800 ms, while the stimulus of next trial emerges at 700 ms, so such experimental design causes distortion of early potential for irrelevant that occurs after relevant. Another issue also stem from the overlapping epochs. The late period potential is affected by the following stimulus.

Moreover, response-evoked potential also shows issue especially when the stimulus is **<font color = 'red'>terminated</font>** by that response (in that experiment design, you may present the stimulus while asking subject do something. e.g., "press space when you see the odd ball"). In this case, a visual change such as a blank screen inevitable affects the signal. However, even if we don't allow the response to terminate the stimulus, the signal is still contaminated by motor preparation and execution, making it hard for us to distinguish whether the difference is due to the stimulus or response.

In a word, we need to be careful with **<font color = 'red'>illsory difference</font>** and to put the ERPs into their physical context.

#### Which ERP component is affected

ERP 成分是「潜成分」(latent components)，不是你看到的波形本身

你看到的波形形状 $\neq$ 成分本身的真实形状

潜在成分会重叠，建议用奥卡姆剃刀

The observed potential is shaped by how we define a ROI. We may operationalize P2 is a potential from 230 - 270 ms. But attention, this time window is decided by youself, thereby you should know to what extent this window also contains other signal/components (e.g., P3 maybe in range of 250 - 330 ms). Therefore, this is about a problem that, **<font color = 'red'>EEG is a sum of massive neural activities, and the collected data is the sum of multiple latent components</font>**. As the figure 10.8 demonstrated, such sum feature genuinely changes what we can see about N2. The true temporal ROI should be slightly later than we observed.

![**Fig 10.8** ERP is resulted from massive latent components](./note_image/Ch10_latent.png)

<br>

#### Comparing ERPs with different number of epochs

在比较 ERP 波形形状或峰值大小时，潜伏期（latency）差异会造成严重问题。

当你把很多试次平均成 ERP 时，如果这些试次的成分出现时间不一致（latency variability），平均后的波形就会：峰值变矮（peak magnitude ↓）、波形变宽（fatter）、整体变平（flatter）。

当你比较 ERP 波形或峰值时，潜伏期差异会让你看到误导性的视觉差异（flattening、smearing），所以必须用更稳健的指标或方法来处理。

latent EEG = neural/psychological cause + physical/artifacial cause. This brings a situation that a peak may occur at $x$ ms for current trial, and occurs at $y$ ms in another epoch/trial. So averaging these epoch together inevitably distorts/flattens the signal as the latency varies for some reasons. Try to make the number of epoch equivalent between conditions when doing the comparison.

> "Or to put it as an easy-to-remember rule: the more epochs within an ERP, the fatter and flatter it will be".

Back to current experiment, the number of epochs follows: `irr` > `rel` > `odd`. SO, be careful.

- delete the `irr` trial until it's equalized
- single trial measures
- analyze the average potential instead of peak value

# Ch11 Inferential statistics and reporting results

This chapter is about doing inference a general rule for a population given data from a experiment sample, using statistical (quantitative) method.

## Exporting data

What we did in the chapter 9 and chapter 10 is preparation to find/define a ROI with particular latency and spatial distribution, allowing us to calculate the final measurement.

ROI helps to operationalize abstract P3 component into a metric. Two ways to select a ROI:

- literature-based
- data-driven

However, the previous practice requires caution: we can't see the plot in Ch10 and define P3 is average potential from 300 - 350 ms over `Pz` (this is a ROI), then calculate p value between that time window at the group level. Such is a questionable research practice as we **<font color = 'red'>double-dipped</font>** our data: <u>doing hypothesis-exploration and hypothesis-testing using ***the same data set***</u>. So how to choose a ROI correctly?

In the chapter 10, Spapé chose two ROIs involving frontal (from 270 - 350 ms) and centro-parietal (from 370 - 800 ms) regions, although the specific channels will be redefined as some participant didn't have some electrodes. These two ROIs answered the first two questions below, while remaining the last one:

- [x] `When`: The selected electrodes

- [x] `Where`: The selected time window/latency

- [ ] `What`: What metric to be used 

  - Global peak, not so good
  - Local peak, sensitive to high frequency noisy, low-pass filter helps with cost
  - Averaged amplitude, robust
  - Area under curve (AUC), robust
  
\begin{align}
\text{Mean amplitude} &= \frac{1}{N} \sum \limits_{1}^{N} V_i \\
\text{Area under curve} &= \int_{t_1}^{t_2} V(t) dt
\end{align}

Although it's widely known that $\int$ seems more precise than $\sum$, it would have such great difference between these two at the resample rate of 512 Hz.

### Using MATLAB to export data

What a shame, visualization by excell (2333:

![**Fig 11.3** Goal of export](./note_image/Ch11_goal_export.png)

I just directly use the "harder" method in Spapé's book.

```{MATLAB Ch11_exporting, eval = F}
% 为了能够进行下去教程，不得不将11章的数据全部覆盖
% 但是我不确定我那个插值是否有问题，最后全tm70个通道了
% 不过实际实验谁tm会用那么极端的情况啊，被试通道数都tm不一样


%%
% 用于循环的准备好变量列表
participant = {
    'umeeg101', 'umeeg102', 'umeeg103', 'umeeg104', ...
    'umeeg105', 'umeeg106', 'umeeg107'
    };

conditions = {
    'rel', 'irr', 'odd'; 
    '201', '202', '203'};

channels = {
    'FC1', 'Cz', 'FC2';  % ROI 1
    'CP1', 'Pz', 'CP2'   % ROI 2
    };

path = '/Users/cheng/Desktop/EEG_study/data_for_study/Chapter 11/data';


%%

% 先给这个循环加个计数功能
count = 0; %用来显示当前所在循环数
total = size(participant, 2) * size(conditions, 2) * size(channels, 1) * size(channels, 2);

% 然后这个空列表用来放置数据
% 因为这个表格我们同时有存字符和数值，所以用cell
% 必须初始化cell的尺寸
% 只是 out_data = {}就是一个1*1的空cell，它不会自动拓展
out_data = cell(512 + 1, total);

for cperson = 1:size(participant, 2)
    for ccond = 1:size(conditions, 2)

        % 数据应该从这里加载
        cEEG = pop_loadset( ...
            'filename', ...
            [participant{cperson} '_11_' conditions{1, ccond} '.set'], ...
            'filepath', path);

        for cROI = 1:size(channels, 1)
            for cchan = 1:size(channels, 2)

                % 数据应该在这里提取然后录入list
                % 首先确定当前通道的号码
                chan_num = find(strcmp({cEEG.chanlocs.labels}, ...
                    channels(cROI, cchan)));
                % 然后把该被试这个通道此条件下的电位平均以后提取出来
                temp_data = mean(cEEG.data(chan_num, :, :), 3);


                % 写入单个cell单元格的时候用{}
                out_data{1, count + 2} = [participant{cperson} '_' conditions{1, ccond} '_ROI' num2str(cROI) '_' channels{cROI, cchan}];
                
                % 写入多个单元格的时候（不是512个数值吗）用()
                out_data(2:end, count + 2) = num2cell(temp_data);
                
                % 写个进度条显示
                count = count + 1;
                fprintf('current pregress: %.2f %% \n', 100 * count/total)
            end
        end
    end
end


% 最后加上时间数据
out_data{1, 1} = 'time';
out_data(2:end, 1) = num2cell(cEEG.times);


%%
% 最后导出数据

% 这是导出为txt
writecell(out_data, './erp_data.txt', 'Delimiter', '\t'); % \t是txt制表符

% 这是导出为csv
writecell(out_data, './erp_data.csv', 'Delimiter', ',');
```

## Spreadsheet

read_delim(

### Peak magnitudes and latency

I still use `R`.

```{r Ch11_magnitude_max}
read_delim(
  file = './data_for_study/self_study/export_data/erp_data.csv', 
  delim = ',', 
  show_col_types = F
) %>% 
  filter(time > 270 & time < 600) %>% 
  select(
    contains('umeeg101') & contains('Cz'), 
    time
    ) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = -time, 
               values_to = 'potential', 
               names_to = 'cond') %>% 
  group_by(cond) %>% 
  slice_max(potential, n = 1)
```

However, this method often fails as it can just detect the global maximum within a certain time range (always falls into the **border** of time range), while the local maximum needs more advanced method such as `pracma::peak()`. Otherwise, visually inspect the plot of each column and change the time range to be processed by `slice_max()`.

the output of `pracma::peak()` is a matrix with the structure:

|peak value|peak index|start index|end index|
|---|---|---|---|
|-0.532623100|18|1|39|
|...|...|...|...|

```{r Ch11_local_max}
# 加载包
library(pracma)

# 首先创建所需的数据框，似乎还是需要长格式的
df <- read_delim(
  file = './data_for_study/self_study/export_data/erp_data.csv', 
  delim = ',', 
  show_col_types = F
) %>% 
  filter(time > 270 & time < 600) %>% 
  select(
    contains('umeeg101') & contains('Cz'), 
    time
    ) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = -time, 
               values_to = 'potential', 
               names_to = 'cond')


# 为了示范，我们先使用一个被试的Cz通道irr条件的电位
df <- df %>% 
  filter(cond == 'umeeg101_irr_ROI1_Cz')

# 然后这里是findpeaks的基本用法
# 输出的矩阵
pracma::findpeaks(
  df$potential,  #作用列
  minpeakheight = mean(df$potential) + sd(df$potential),  #一个峰最小要达到多大
  minpeakdistance = 20,  #峰之间至少要间隔多少个采样点。
  npeaks = 1  #返回几个峰
  )

# 然后EEG不是还有负峰吗，所以对应解决方法就是，取负数找
pracma::findpeaks(- df$potential)
```

So how to automatically find the peak of each conditions and of each channel? I tried to combine `pracma::findpeaks` with `summarize`.

```{r Ch11_local_peak}
# 同样的先准备好长数据
# 假设我们只搞ROI1的数据
df <- read_delim(
  file = './data_for_study/self_study/export_data/erp_data.csv', 
  delim = ',', 
  show_col_types = F
) %>% 
  filter(time > 270 & time < 350) %>% 
  select(
    contains('ROI1'), 
    time
    ) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = -time, 
               values_to = 'potential', 
               names_to = c('subject', 'cond', 'ROI', 'chan'), 
               names_sep = '_') %>% 
  select(-ROI)


# 然后数据应该得分一下组
# 负峰的就先略
df %>% 
  group_by(chan, cond) %>% 
  summarize(
    pos_peak = {
      p <- pracma::findpeaks(potential, 
                             minpeakheight = mean(potential) + sd(potential), 
                             minpeakdistance = 20, 
                             npeak = 1)
      
      if (is.null(p)) NA else p[1,1]
    }, 
    pos_latency = {
      p <- pracma::findpeaks(potential, 
                             minpeakheight = mean(potential) + sd(potential), 
                             minpeakdistance = 20, 
                             npeak = 1)
      
      if (is.null(p)) NA else time[p[1,2]]
    }, 
    .groups = "drop_last"
  )
```

### Crafting ERP figures

Ha! data visualization with `R`!

```{r Ch11_ERP_plot}
# 假如我们只可视化Cz通道ROI1的数据
df <- read_delim(

  delim = ',',

) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = -time,

  ggplot() + 
    geom_line(aes(x = time, y = grand_erp, color = cond)) +

    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +

    theme_classic() + 
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + 
    scale_color_discrete(
      name = 'Conditions', 
      labels = c('irr' = 'Irrelevant', 
                 'rel' = 'Relevant', 
                 'odd' = 'Odd ball'), 
      breaks = c('irr', 'rel', 'odd')
    )
```

**<font color = 'red'>Any accidental difference in waveform compared to that in the tutorial is due to the fucking interpolation for our data with extreme situation that participants have varying channel number!</font>**

Although creating a plot is not quite hard, there are some tips on **<font color = 'red'>graph design</font>** advised by Spapé.

1. A plot should be about <u>8.5 cm</u> and the text should be not smaller than <u>7 pt</u>.

2. Note everything necessary down clearly (e.g., the legend, x and y labels).

3. Use as no more then **<font color = 'red'>3</font>** lines as possible in a single plot.

4. When demonstrating plots of multiple channels, eliminate some redundant element such as shared x axis and legend.

5. Make sure the plots follow the same/consistent format (e.g., ERP line with same width and plot with same size).

  ) %>%

head(df)

### One-way deisgn

```{r Ch11_load_package, include=FALSE}
library(bruceR)
```

I just found that long format data is easier to be operated in ANOVA.

```{r Ch11_one-wa, eval = F}
# library(bruceR)
# 这个语法是用于长数据格式，说实话感觉更方便比书上的宽格式
MANOVA(df, subID = 'subject', dv = 'potential', within = 'cond')

# 然后事后检验
lm <- MANOVA(df, subID = 'subject', dv = 'potential', within = 'cond')
lm %>% 
  EMMEANS(effect = 'cond')
```

**<font color = 'red'>Any accidental difference in results compared to those in the tutorial is due to the fucking interpolation for our data with extreme situation that participants have varying channel number!</font>**

Remember the data should not violate the **<font color = 'red'>sphericity assumption</font>**, otherwise use `sph.correction="GG" (or ="HF")` in the function `MANOVA()`.

Then we can write the result section based on the number we get from the code above, if everything run correctly. Spapé suggested to make each part as concise as possible because the result section is easy to get explosion.

### Multi-factorial designs

The interaction effect in EEG research is ubiquitous since the neural events are naturally specific to certain time window and electrodes (e.g., some activation only occurs within particular time and regions while it stay in silence in other time and regions). So, as the result, the interaction is very common in EEG data.

```{r Ch11_multi-factor, eval = F}
# 准备数据，得多搞出来一个时间范围的变量
df <- read_delim(
  file = './data_for_study/self_study/export_data/erp_data.csv', 
  delim = ',', 
  show_col_types = F
) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = - time, 
               values_to = 'potential', 
               names_to = c('subject', 'cond', 'ROI', 'chan'), 
               names_sep = '_') %>% 
  filter((time > 270 & time < 350) | 
         (time > 370 & time < 600)) %>% 
  select(- ROI) %>% 
  mutate(timerange = ifelse(time < 360, 'time_1', 'time_2'))

# 果然还是长格式好用
lm <- bruceR::MANOVA(df, subID = 'subject', 
                     dv = 'potential', 
                     within = c('cond', 'timerange', 'chan'), 
                     # 这个用来修正方差不齐
                     sph.correction="GG")

lm %>% 
  bruceR::EMMEANS(effect = 'cond', by = c('timerange', 'chan'))
```

So what's the meaning of these result numbers?

Pertaining to how express and arrange these numbers, Spapé gave an example that leaves non-significant and non-interested items out of the result section. Attention, the value difference exists between mine and that in the text below.

> "In repeated measures ANOVA with relevance (relevant vs irrelevant vs odd), time (T1 vs T2), and electrode (Cz vs Pz) as factor, and average amplitude as dependent, relevance and time had significant main effects, ps < .002, while electrode did not. More interestingly, time and relevance also interacted, F (1, 6) = 101.32, p < .0001, with the later effect of relevance being far larger (T2 rel = 0.90 µV, T2 irr = -0.57 µV) than the early effect (-0.41 vs -0.93). Relevance also interacted with electrode, with the effect of relevance being more visible on the Pz (Pz: Rel 0.46 µV vs irr -0.66 µV) than Cz (0.03 µV vs -0.84 µV). Finally, the three-way interaction was also significant, F (1, 6) = 21.88, p = .003. This showed that the early relevance effect was more pronounced in Cz (rel–irr = 0.71 µV) than Pz (rel-irr = 0.34 µV), while the later relevance effect was reversed, and weaker over Cz (1.02 µV) than Pz (rel-irr = 1.92 µV)."

Spapé didn't use the result of post-hoc test because: 1. he only used two levels for each factor in the tutorial; 2. cherry-picking problem that he would go in detail later.

Besides, the logic in the last sentence of the example text is worthy to learn about. How to translate a 3-way interaction result into that description? The tip is "**<font color = 'red'>understand interaction as differences of differences</font>**". For example, if the temperature is the dependent variable, and we have a interaction between continent (EU vs China), region (city vs village), and season (summer vs winter), we first get the 8 temperature values for each condition ($2^3$ conditions). We further can subtract winter temperature from summer, getting 4 values then. Again, by subtracting city from village, we finally get only 2 values to be compared. At this step, if this pair of difference in temperature is noticible, we could say "the summer-winter difference is smaller in EU city compared to EU village, while this effect reversed in China". Well, I need a step-by-step operation to make sure I have understand:

$$
\text{continent} \times \text{region} \times \text{season}
$$

1. For every $\text{continent} \times \text{region}$, subtracting winter from summer temperature:
    - EU city's seasonal difference
    
    - EU village's seasonal difference
    
    - CN city's seasonal difference
    
    - CN village's seasonal difference
  
2. For every continents, $\text{diff}_{\text{city}} - \text{diff}_{\text{village}}$.
    - EU's region difference
    
    - CN's region difference
  
3. Comparing the region difference in temperature between continents, write down the conclusion.

However, things get far more complicated then the factor has more than 2 levels. Fuck. Moreover, the method we used to pick up ROI and to analyze the data so far is actually **<font color = 'red'>problematic</font>**. This is about the content of next section.

## Methodological issues in EEG research

The problem in our previous analysis is that, we selected ROI by looking at the waveform, the data, and tested the same data again. This is invalid since all picked data has agree with our assumption before testing. A sort of **<font color = 'red'>confirmation bias</font>**

Cherry picking is to exclude non-significant sample out of analysis. Selecting prefered electrodes and time range is kinds of that, to some extent. Pre-processing is necessary and ROI selection as well. The point is how to avoid abuse these method and practice.

### HARKing

Examining the hypothesis, don't explore the hypothesis. In other words, please don't change your hypothesis based on your data results. On the other aspect, it requires us to write the hypothesis clearly before looking at data. The worse thing is that after picking up the "right" hypothesis, we turn into the literature and borrow support from them and pretending our "right" hypothesis is reasonable from at first. That's methodological revisionism.

### Double-dipping

**<font color = 'red'>Drawing a target after shooting</font>** is illegal, that's scattershot approach. Again it back to the hypothesis exploration topic. Namely conduct tests across all dataset and just pick up the that with significant results to report. So it's do first test (maybe it's not a formal statistics for this roll) to decide where the second one should be placed, with maximized significance.

如果事先没有明确假设，但是结果里出现了某个模式，当然可以提出可能的解释，但是要声明这是有待进一步研究的，探索性的假设。

### Type I & type II errors

Apart from the problem of cherry picking and double dipping, even if we strictly conduct analysis, we still get 64 channels $\times$ 512 timepoints = 32768 chances that committing type I error: incorrectly refusing null hypothesis. Specifically, if we want to test whether here's a difference between 2 conditions on this dataset, using a simple paired t-test with a threshold of 0.0001 (in eeglab's `Study > plot`), in sum the probability of type I error is by:

$$
1 - 0.9999^{32768} \approx 0.96
$$

Quite high.

The opposite side, type II error, incorrectly accepting null hypothesis, is also dangerous. It's arising from over-controlling for type I error.

### Strategies to avoid QRP

It's important to keep in mind that, even we have observed a potential evoked by A, which is similar with that triggered by B, we still need to be careful to say "A causes the same effect as B". That's because different cognitive processing still can generate the same EEG measurement.

Moreover, it's easy to find a lot of research with related results has been done and we misunderstand they got a consensus. This leads us to use a more forgiving statistical threshold instead of a threshold required based on our total data.

The principle is to read the original literature -> conduct test (maybe not formal statistics) -> test a specific ROI. And we shall do things below to let reviewers know that we followed a healthy academic pipeline.

1. Pre-register
- <osf.com>

- Do just what we have done for the course project in the first semester.

2. Distinguish exploratory and confirmatory analysis in paper: 
- The part we have mentioned in the pre-registration is "confirmatory analysis"

- The test beyond the part you mentioned in pre-registration is "exploratory analysis".

3. Data with exploratory and confirmatory analysis.
    1. Splitting data
    - Something sounds like training set and testing set in machine learning? 
    
    - Use the data from a small group of sample as the "pilot group" to explore the pattern, effect, and ROI and confirm the result on the main group.
    
    2. Separate procedure
    - Select ROI of main effect by **exploratory** and <u>then</u> test the interaction between primary and secondary factors by **confirmatory**.
    
    - Once a exception occurs (e.g., the interaction located outside the ROI), an extra exploratory analysis is okay, while incorporate new channels or new time window into the ROI is cheating.

4. Report null effects
- Bayesian method is recommended, using `JASP`

## Frequency field analysis

### General principle

$$
sin(2 \pi \cdot f \cdot t + \varphi)
$$

f = frequency

t = time

$\varphi$ = phase

f $\times$ t = current cycle

time field -> amplitude spectrum + phase spectrum


```{r E1_fft_demo}
# if we have a recorded signal containing 3 sources
srate <- 512
duration <- 2
n <- srate * duration

time <- seq(0, duration, length.out = n)

sig_1 <- sin(2 * pi * 2 * time)
sig_2 <- 2 * sin(2 * pi * 20 * time)
sig_3 <- 3 * sin(2 * pi * 40 * time)
sig_4 <- 5 * sin(2 * pi * 70 * time)

sig <- sig_1 + sig_2 + sig_3 + sig_4

# so the signal looks like this in the time field
plot(time, sig, 'l')

# if we administer Fourier transformation onto this signal
ori <- fft(sig)

# Mod()和abs()对于fft结果等效
#sum(Mod(power) == abs(power)) / length(Mod(power) == abs(power))

# 提取振幅信息
# 别忘了乘2除以n
amplitude <- abs(ori) * 2 / n

# 然后不知道为啥fft的结果只有前一半是实信号
# Nyquist freqg

# calculate the frequency vector, it's just a formula
freq <- (0:(n/2)) * srate / n
plot(freq, amplitude[1:(n/2 + 1)], 'l')
```

However the question is, EEG signal isn't so tidy and regular. In other words, EEG signal is not periodic time series. One solution is to decompose EEG into more components with continuously increasing frequency and smaller separation. This actually regards EEG as a signal having a very slow cycle (e.g., the whole EEG is only 1 cycle).

Another issue involves **<font color = 'red'>Nyquist frequency</font>**. Just giving up the frequency band beyond a certain threshold, by which the signal becomes "fake" due to something about sample rate. So we can only use the first half part of `fft()`'s result.

Luckily, I have used `fft()` when I tried to make EEG music, though some Nyquist details are needed to be added in that script.

### Power measures

We have convert time field inforation into that in the frequency field, with the amplitude remained. But the power (功率) measure or power spectral density (PSD, 功率谱密度) are widely used in the EEG research as well.

\begin{align}
\text{Amplitude: } &\mu v
\text{power: } &\mu v^2
\text{PSD: } &\frac{\text{power}}{\text{sample rate}}
\text{PSD (dB): } &10 log_{10} \text{PSD}
\end{align}

```{r power_freq}
power <- 2 * abs(ori)^2  / n
plot(freq, power[1:(n/2 + 1)], 'l')

PSD <- power / srate
plot(freq, PSD[1:(n/2 + 1)], 'l')

db <- 10 * log(PSD, base = 10)
plot(freq, db[1:(n/2 + 1)], 'l')
```

### Analysis

The statistical thing for frequency field is broadly same with that for time field. Some skills are noted in the code chunk below.

```{MATLAB freq_field_ana}
% 初始化
clc; clear all;

% 设置路径
cd('/Users/cheng/Desktop/EEG_study/data_for_study/self_study/freq_ana');


%%
% 这里首先是之前频域分析里面的内容，思路看rmarkdown笔记
% 我们直接看怎么应用到eeglab数据里
% 一般频域分析都是用在静息态数据里的
% 这里就假设cond维度记录的不是条件，而是分段

% eeglab

% 首先加载数据
participants = {'umeeg101', 'umeeg102', 'umeeg103', 'umeeg104', ...
                'umeeg105', 'umeeg106', 'umeeg107'};

cond = {'rel', 'irr', 'odd'};


% 正确的fft逻辑是先按通道将数据傅立叶变换，但是不要叠加
% 把一个个体所有数据傅立叶变换以后再叠加，最后汇总为一个组的频域数据
for cpar = 1:length(participants)
    for ccond = 1:length(cond)

        % 加载数据
        EEG = pop_loadset('filename', ...
                          [participants{cpar} '_11_' cond{ccond} '.set'], ...
                          'filepath', ...
                          '/Users/cheng/Desktop/EEG_study/data_for_study/Chapter 11/data');

        % 然后每个数据都是通道 * 时间 * 试次
        % 原封不动fft，不要叠加
        for cepoch = 1:size(EEG.data, 3)
            for cchan = 1:size(EEG.data, 1)

                % 先准备一个傅立叶变化的“重采样”，这个是优化计算的步骤
                % 这个主要是找到离本来采样率最近的2的次幂数
                NFFT = 2^nextpow2(EEG.srate);

                % 开始fft，用一个临时变量存储每一个通道的数据
                temp = fft(EEG.data(cchan, :, cepoch), NFFT);
                temp = abs(temp);

                % 然后记录一下一个个体的振幅
                cEEG(cchan, :, cepoch) = temp .* 2 ./ length(temp);
            end
        end

        % 保存数据，这个时候再平均叠加
        % 被试；条件；通道；频率
        ALL(cpar, ccond, :, :) = squeeze(mean(cEEG, 3));

        % 清除缓存
        clear temp; clear cEEG;
    end
end

disp('done')


% 计算频率list
% NFFT = size(ALL, 4)都是fft的采样率
freq = (0:(NFFT - 1)) * EEG.srate / NFFT;

% 然后看一看前50个频率在第一个通道的组水平振幅
% 无视条件信息，仅为代码演示方便
% 其他的功率什么的套公式就是
group = squeeze(mean(ALL, [1 2]));

figure;
plot(freq(1:50), group(1, 1:50));


% 当然也可以直接看整个Nyquist频率
% 这里仍然用第一个通道作为演示
group = squeeze(mean(ALL, [1 2]));

figure;
nyquist = NFFT / 2 + 1;
plot(freq(1:nyquist), group(1, 1:nyquist));

%%
% 然后用这个频域信息，我用的是振幅，画地形图
group;

count = 0;

for i = 0:5:35
    count = count + 1;
    segment = find(freq >= i & freq <= i + 5);
    plot_amplitude = squeeze(mean(group(:, segment), 2));
    subplot(2, 4, count)

    % 然后maplimits这个参数怎么用还是没有搞懂
    topoplot(plot_amplitude, EEG.chanlocs, ...
             'electrodes', 'on', ...
             'maplimits', 'absmax');
    title([num2str(freq(segment(1))) '-' num2str(freq(segment(end))) ' Hz'])
    colorbar;
end


%%
% 频域统计分析和时域的统计分析在代码形式上一致
% 不过要是想在r里用的舒服点估计还是得弄出个带表头的数据
```
